video_title: What the Hell Just Happened?! | Animal Spirits 490
gist: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick dissect the post-2026-midterm whipsaw: a Democratic wave and 43-of-44 ballot rejections of data centers sparked fears for AI capex, followed by the Nasdaq 100's worst day since 2020 (semis -11%, South Korea -14%) driven largely by hedge-fund leverage, then a rebound. They also cover Nvidia key-man risk after Jensen's Chinese-spy affair, SpaceX/AWS growth targets, falling rates normalizing bond spreads, and dot-com-era evidence that ex-tech stocks can hedge an AI unwind.

insights.claim: In the Thursday after the 2026 midterms the S&P 500 fell more than 4%, the Nasdaq almost 6%, emerging markets 6%, semiconductor stocks 11% and South Korea 14% in a single day — the Nasdaq 100's worst drop since March 2020, wiping out over $2 trillion.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Scale of the AI-led drawdown frames how levered global markets (Korea, EM, semis) are to the AI trade.
insights.quote: Semiconductor stocks were down 11% and South Korea was down 14% in a day.

insights.claim: At the post-election Thursday close, South Korean stocks were down 40% from highs, semiconductors down a third, the momentum factor (MTUM) down almost 30%, emerging markets near a bear market, while the S&P 500 was only down about 6% and Europe about 5%.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Damage is concentrated in AI/momentum exposures; index-level losses understate pain in crowded factors and AI-linked countries.

insights.claim: Citing Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer: AI stocks were down 30% from highs while equal-weight S&P was down only 1.3% and the S&P ex-AI was up 0.5%, showing investors rotate within equities rather than going to cash.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Selloffs are mega-rotations, not de-risking; equal-weight and ex-AI exposure has been an effective hedge.
insights.quote: They don't want to go to cash yet.

insights.claim: The initial overnight futures selloff (Nasdaq down ~3% after hours) on a Democratic 'blue wave' was rational because Republicans are likelier to support data-center spending and much AI capex is committed in Texas; the next-day rally was also rational because slower, extended capex reduces cash burn at the hyperscalers.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Political outcomes now map directly onto AI capex expectations; slower capex can be read as bullish for free cash flow.
insights.quote: Doesn't everybody hate the fact that these cash cows are now bleeding cash?

insights.claim: The violent Thursday drop and Monday rebound are best explained by positioning and leverage — overlevered hedge funds blowing up and forced selling — rather than any fundamental narrative.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Leverage-driven drawdowns tend to round-trip quickly; distinguish forced selling from fundamental repricing.
insights.quote: a bunch of hedge funds were overleveraged. They sold out that caused the market to fall and then rebound, that's not very exciting.

insights.claim: A JP Morgan chart shows hedge funds degrossing to the biggest extent since 2016, alongside Bloomberg headlines of hedge funds plunging 30% and cutting staff.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Record degrossing typically marks a positioning washout that can precede rebounds.

insights.claim: Hedge funds may be the new 'dumb money' because they run heavy leverage in the same crowded AI bets, possibly with more herding as funds hand decisions to AI.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Crowded-trade risk is elevated; watch for correlated deleveraging events.
insights.quote: is this the new are they the new dumb money?

insights.claim: Even a perfectly correct macro AI thesis (e.g., the 'Situational Awareness' author) can fail if leverage prevents surviving drawdowns until the thesis plays out.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Size positions to survive volatility; being right on direction is insufficient with leverage.

insights.claim: Market cycles are compressing: a full cycle of narrative and price action played out across just two to three days around the election.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Expect faster reversals; short-term narrative trading is increasingly whipsaw-prone.

themes.theme: Semis and memory: priced for peak

insights.claim: Per Warren Pies, cumulatively the S&P 500 is up 71% on days when semiconductors (SMH) rise and down 34% on days they fall in 2026 — a 105% spread showing the market is driven almost entirely by whether AI is 'good or bad' that day.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Index returns are effectively a semiconductor bet; diversification within the S&P is lower than it appears.
insights.quote: There's a 105% spread. This is nutso.

insights.claim: Round Hill's memory ETF DRAM, a concentrated semiconductor bet more volatile than SMH, was down 54% at last week's lows and remains 48% below its highs.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Memory names have already been massacred; gauge of how much cycle-peak risk is priced in.

insights.claim: SanDisk is trading at about three times earnings because the market believes memory earnings are at a cyclical peak.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Extremely low multiples signal disbelief in earnings durability — a potential setup if earnings stay strong longer.
insights.quote: SanDisk is trading for three times earnings.

insights.claim: Michael Batnick thinks the market has been right to look through peak memory earnings and finds an upward re-rating of memory expectations very improbable, crediting the market for usually getting cycle peaks right.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Argues against bottom-fishing cheap memory stocks on trailing P/E.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson raises the risk that AI demand (e.g., SpaceX revenue targets) is massively underestimated, which would force semiconductor estimates higher and could eventually produce a blow-off top; Michael Batnick counters that the market is 'so far from blowoff top'.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Upside earnings surprise in semis is the bull tail to watch given depressed sentiment.
insights.quote: what if there is a major underestimation and that's when we get like the blowoff top

insights.claim: Voters rejected data centers in every ballot measure except one (roughly 43 of 44 measures), signaling local resistance to AI infrastructure buildout.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Rising local opposition is a new cost/timing risk for AI infrastructure projects.

insights.claim: Ben Carlson expects the data-center backlash to raise build costs (taxes, incentives, more remote sites) and lower ROI rather than stop the buildout, ultimately entrenching hyperscalers that can afford to pay up.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Higher entry costs favor the largest balance sheets; marginal smaller builders lose.
insights.quote: Doesn't this just mean the hyperscalers are going to win and just pay pay a little bit more for it?

insights.claim: Meta President Dina Powell McCormick said a newly elected governor who campaigned against data centers privately asked to meet after inauguration so the state would not lose Meta's investment and jobs.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Campaign rhetoric against data centers may soften in practice; capex risk from the election may be overstated.

insights.claim: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says AWS, at a $184 billion run rate growing 39%, could grow ~40% a year for the next two years and become a trillion-plus business, justifying aggressive capex despite investor preference for slower spending.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler capex intent remains intact; AWS growth guidance underpins AI infrastructure demand.
insights.quote: we're going to invest to continue to be the leader.

insights.claim: Michael Batnick argues the election-driven slowdown in AI capex is a positive: the AI trade is not over, just more palatable for investors, and CEOs would likely be thrilled to spread spending over longer periods.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Slower capex could improve FCF and support re-rating of hyperscalers.
insights.quote: the AI trade is not done. It's just going to be more palatable for investors.

insights.claim: Elon Musk told Ron Baron that SpaceX will hit a $100 billion annualized revenue run rate by December and could reach $500 billion next year.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: If realized, implies AI/compute demand far above current estimates, supporting semis earnings.

insights.claim: Investors punish mega-caps like Meta when they need to raise capital despite years of buybacks and dividends, as seen when Mark Zuckerberg sought funding for AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: External financing of AI capex is a stock-price headwind; watch funding announcements.

insights.claim: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized for an affair with a woman reported to be a Chinese spy tied to a company intertwined with Nvidia, yet Nvidia stock fell only about 4-5%.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Key-man and governance risk at the most important AI company appears under-priced.

insights.claim: Dan Ives said that if Jensen Huang is removed as CEO, Nvidia would be worth 20-30% less; a short seller had previously published a report on Nvidia's China ties.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Quantifies key-man discount; CEO-change headlines would be a large downside catalyst.

insights.claim: With Democrats now controlling Congress, the Jensen Huang affair could trigger months of investigations into potential leakage of secrets to China, making it a significant ongoing risk for Nvidia.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Regulatory/political overhang on Nvidia and China chip-export policy may intensify.
insights.quote: There's going to be investigations out the ass for months and months to come on this.

insights.claim: Elon Musk carries more key-man risk than anyone in history; his net worth fell over $100 billion after the election as Tesla and SpaceX values dropped.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Musk-linked assets embed concentrated founder risk.

insights.claim: Since 2010 the US stock market is up almost 800% versus 22% for China, which Ben Carlson frames as a reason China resorts to espionage to catch up in AI.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Long-run US equity outperformance vs China persists; tech competition is a geopolitical risk factor.

insights.claim: Per Bespoke, over the last year the Nasdaq 100 has spent more time in a 10%+ correction than in a rally, and it has had about seven 10% corrections since 2022 while still rising.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Frequent double-digit drawdowns are normal in this regime; avoid over-reacting to each one.

insights.claim: With rates falling over the past month, cash yields have lost their edge and fixed income (short-term, corporate, core, multisector, high yield, tax-equivalent munis) now offers positive spreads over cash — a normal bond market for the first time in a long time.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Supports rotating idle cash into duration and credit as cash yields decline.
insights.quote: this is a normal fixed income market finally for the first time in a very long time.

insights.claim: After the dot-com bust, while the Nasdaq fell ~80%, the S&P 500 ex-tech and telecom had a positive return from peak to trough, with small caps, mid caps and value doing well.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: If AI unwinds, ex-tech, small/mid caps and value are historically effective hedges.
insights.quote: Xtech and Telecom had a positive return.

insights.claim: If money leaves tech for good, the abundant liquidity sloshing around will likely rotate into sectors like staples and financials rather than leave equities.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Position for sector rotation, not broad de-risking, in an AI unwind.

insights.claim: US unemployment has been below 5% for 61 consecutive months, approaching the record 64-month streak of 1965-1970 and likely to break it.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Labor market remains resilient; AI has not yet disrupted employment in aggregate.

themes.theme: Politics, populism and the global investor

insights.claim: The 2026 midterms were a repudiation of billionaire influence: Elon Musk spent roughly $200-400 million and about 98% of his backed candidates lost, while young men under 30 swung from heavily Republican to Democrat.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Political narratives flip fast; 'top vs bottom' populism raises regulatory risk for big tech and billionaires.

insights.claim: The election was framed as less left vs right than top vs bottom, with public antipathy toward AI leaders (Musk, Zuckerberg, Altman) fueling demand for a reckoning and rooting for an AI crash.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Anti-tech-elite sentiment is a political tailwind for AI regulation and data-center opposition.
insights.quote: this election was way less about the left and the right as it was versus the top and the bottom.

insights.claim: New York Times stock fell 3% the day after the election on a day when nearly every other stock rallied.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Media stocks may suffer when their political focus loses salience.

insights.claim: Young investors globally (e.g., Italy) are taking responsibility for their own finances as pension promises erode, implying the US 'relentless bid' for equities will become a global, multi-year flow story.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson
insights.so_what: Structural global retail inflows into equities could support valuations for years.
insights.quote: That is going to be a global story and it's already starting.
